title: Slow English Storytime 🇰🇷🇺🇸 | Growing Up Korean American
channel: Speak English with Bo's Slow English

lines.text: Hi, how are you? My name is Bo and this
is Bo's Slow English. Today, I want to
continue talking about my life and
experience as a Korean-American.
I received a lot of positive feedback on
one of my recent videos where I talked
about being Korean-American and my
identity or identity. I have several
private students and some of them live
in Seoul, South Korea and I've been
trying to get in touch with my culture
more lately.
When I say get in touch, I mean to
relate to it more and to embrace it
more. First of all, there are several
things that Koreans find strange about
America. For example, small talk. Lots
of small talk with strangers. I would
like to say I am maybe the queen of
small talk because of all the years of
experience I have working in customer
service. Not only customer service, but
it is luxury customer service. So, it is
kind of a requirement to build a rapport
with someone or with the client. When I
say rapport, I mean a relationship. I
generally make small talk almost
everywhere I go if I'm in the mood for
it. In the morning, early in the
morning, when I take my dog out and I
have to walk around the neighborhood,
naturally, [snorts]
I don't really want to have small talk
because I'm still waking up. But, there
are some neighbors who want to have
small talk with me.
So, things that we might talk about is
"What are your plans for today?"
Or they'll say, "What are your plans for
today?"
"What have you been up to?"
"Did you do anything fun this weekend?"
"Do you have any summer plans?" "Do you
have any summer plans?" I might make
small talk with someone in an elevator.
If the elevator is very quiet, it is
common for people to want to have small
talk almost because Americans are afraid
of silence. Something I find to be
interesting is my dad loves to make
small talk. And I find it to be
interesting because he's very Korean.
Yes, he is a Korean-American,
but
I would say I'm first-generation
Korean-American, and he is very much
still a South Korean in his head. But,
when we are out in public, whether we're
at a restaurant, we're at the train
station, he wants to make small talk.
So, I'm very curious, in your country,
no matter where you live,
do you like to make small talk? Do you
think this is more of a personality
thing, or do you think it's a cultural
thing?
I think it's a little bit of both. In
[snorts] addition to having small talk
with strangers, Americans like to smile
a lot to strangers, and more so in some
parts of the country versus others. For
example, when you walk around Manhattan,
New York City, you're not to see a lot
of people smiling at each other because
you're constantly passing people all day
long. Now, that is just a stereotype,
but that is my observation and my
experience. On the other hand, in my
neighborhood, there are many neighbors
with dogs, and I usually say hi
when I walk by someone, whether I know
them or not. Also,
in America, we tip.
Tipping is part of the culture, and I
know most of the world does not tip.
Growing up working in customer service
since the age of 14, tipping is just
normal for me. And it's also how I was
able to pay my bills. Sometimes in
America, like with waiters, they may
make a lower hourly rate, and they make
the rest of their money through tips.
Another way to say tip is gratuity.
Would you like to add a gratuity? That
sounds more formal and polite
compared to would you like to add a tip?
Gratuity sounds better. I feel like I
grew up
between two cultures.
Sometimes I felt too American.
Sometimes I felt too Korean.
And I myself have had many struggles
when it comes to learning English when I
was younger. As for my family's
expectations of me as a Korean,
to be honest, my parents were very
hands-off.
They were very lenient for being Korean
parents. When I say lenient, I mean the
opposite of strict. So, I had very
lenient parents who allowed me to just
live my life, and I did not have to fit
within specific Korean family
expectations. I remember growing up and
feeling really
embarrassed about my name.
The name Bo was too unique,
and back in the day, it wasn't cool to
be unique.
Nowadays, it is cool to be unique. The
name Bo is part of my Korean name.
My Korean name is Pona.
And I know
for you non-Korean speakers, you're
probably thinking, "Why does your B
sound like a P?" It's like a soft B.
That sounds like a B P.
Pona. So, my Korean name is Pona,
but my English name is Bo.
And I distinctly,
clearly remember when I was
transitioning from elementary school to
middle school, I begged my mom, "Please,
I do not want to go to middle school, to
this brand new school with brand new
students and teachers. I don't want to
tell them my name." I was so scared,
but eventually, I was very much accepted
within a new friends group, and I
realized it was all in my head. I built
it up so much in my head, and I I
myself out for no reason. Now, I am
proud of my name and I also like how my
YouTube name is Bo's Slow English. I
like that it has a little rhyme, Bo and
Slow. I think that's fun. I'm just now
remembering
where my embarrassment started with my
name.
I remember the lunch ladies in
elementary school had a hard time
pronouncing my name.
They would see my name on the card that
had my lunch order and they pronounced
it as Boo.
I don't know why. Maybe because the word
t o is pronounced too and the word b o
was so unique that they just thought,
"Oh,
t o is too, so b o is Boo." So, they
would say my name, "Boo, come get your
lunch."
And I was so embarrassed. So, I'm just
remembering that story and I think
that's part of where my embarrassment
came from.
Currently,
I feel 50% Korean, 50% American. I'm
trying to
embrace my Korean side more and as I
mentioned, I'm learning more about my
culture with having my private students,
but also getting to know some of my
YouTube subscribers. I've also been
watching Korean reality TV shows on
Netflix. I have a really difficult time
understanding what the actors are saying
usually and sometimes I beat myself up
over it, but then I
remembered I need to have some
patience with myself, and that is my
message to you. When you are watching an
English-speaking TV show or movie,
please have patience with yourself. You
will get it at some point, but the more
effort you put into it on a daily basis,
the faster you will become fluent. I
hope you enjoyed today's story about my
life and my Korean American identity.
Please like, subscribe, and share with
your friends, and also check out my new
YouTube channel that's for kids,
families, and super beginner English
learners. See you soon. Bye.
